transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-02 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Patel (Drawbridge VP Eng), Omar Singh (ML Lead), Harriet Cole (SRE)
Links shared: Redwood POC SOW (link), Benchmark template (sheet link), sample logs (s3 link)

Summary:
High-level scoping for a 4-week POC to validate capacity sizing and autoscale behavior for Drawbridge's latency-sensitive customer-facing inference. Focus: reserved GPU baseline for steady traffic, burst pool for peak events, and clear fallback policies to maintain availability under overload. Success criteria: p95 under 350ms for short-chat model, 99.9% availability, and cost per 1k requests target.

Topics covered:
- Current stack & constraints (on-prem + cloud hybrid, strict data controls)
- Workload profile and token lengths (mix of short chat + long summaries)
- Reserved capacity sizes and burst strategy (GPU types discussed)
- Fallback policies (model variants, region failover)
- Benchmarks and required traces / success metrics
- Security & network requirements (KMS, VPC peering, SOC2 notes)

Action items (recap in call): see metadata action_items list above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then we wanna go deep on capacity sizing, is that right Lena?
[00:08] Lena: Yeah hi, thanks. We need to scope a POC so we can prove latency at scale for our chat assistant. Our users expect sub 300–350ms p95 for short prompts, but the workload has long summary jobs too.
[00:18] Diego: Got it. Couple clarifying q's: what's your steady-state QPS and peak bursts? And are you able to share a traffic trace?
[00:25] Omar: Steady is about 120 RPS, peaks up to 1.2k during morning burst windows; token distribution is 70% <60 tokens, 30% 200–800 tokens for nightly batch summaries. We'll drop a sanitized trace.
[00:40] Harriet: Also important: we have a hybrid infra. Customer data can't leave our VPC for critical flows. So private deployment or VPC peering plus KMS must be in scope.
[00:50] Maya: That makes sense. For the POC we typically propose 2 phases: an initial reserved pool to cover steady QPS plus a small burst pool to simulate spikes, then a step where we run benchmark traces and adjust. The reserved vs dedicated wording — we call it Redwood Dedicated for reserved capacity; lmk if the name gets garbled —
[01:05] Omar: Sorry, quick interject — when you say reserved pool, what's the baseline GPU type you're assuming? A100? H100?
[01:12] Diego: For latency-sensitive chat we usually test on A100 or H100 depending on model. For the POC we can provision an A100 baseline and then show H100 delta. We'll include quantized variants where appropriate to hit cost targets.
[01:24] Lena: Our SRE prefers stable predictable latency so reserved capacity is preferred. But we still need burst for holiday spikes — if reserved is full what's the fallback?
[01:34] Maya: Two-tier fallback: first fallback to a compatible quantized model (same weights, lower precision), second fallback to a smaller model family we keep warm in the burst pool, third is region failover if local capacity is exhausted. We'll also set graceful tail-dropping for non-critical batch jobs.
[01:50] Harriet: How are you handling KV cache / prefix caching gar— caching? We rely heavily on reuse across sessions.
[01:56] Diego: Good point. Redwood runtime supports prefix/KV cache and we can show end-to-end with a warmed cache to demonstrate effective latency reductions. The benchmark will include cold and warm paths.
[02:07] Omar: One concern: our summary jobs blow up memory with long sequences. Do you have examples of sequence length handling and kernel selection?
[02:15] Diego: Yes, our compilation and kernel selector picks optimized kernels based on seq length distribution. For long sequences we may need interleaving strategies and larger GPU configs; we'll show perf numbers in the bench runs.
[02:26] Lena: Ok, timeline wise — we want a 4 week POC: week 0 prep, week 1 baseline bench, week 2 burst runs, week 3 final tuning and handoff. Is that close to what you recommend?
[02:36] Maya: Exactly, and we can compress if we get traces earlier. Deliverables: bench report, cost model, capacity recommendation, and rollback/fallback runbook.
[02:45] Harriet: Security: we need KMS integration and audit logs. Is SOC2 attestation available for the hosted route?
[02:51] Maya: Yes, Redwood Hosted is SOC2; private deploy option is for when you need customer-managed KMS and full control. We'll include SSO/SAML and RBAC details in the security packet.
[03:02] Omar: For the bursts, is autoscale immediate? Our concern is the cold-start latency when spinning new worker pods.
[03:09] Diego: Autoscale has a couple knobs: burst buffer (warm standby instances), fast hot pool (keep smaller number of models preloaded) and continuous batching. Cold-starts are mitigated by keeping a minimal warm pool; we can show trade-offs.
[03:20] Lena: Pricing question — reserved capacity monthly commit vs pay-as-you-go during POC — how do you present cost?
[03:27] Maya: For POC we do a temporary reserved commit at a discounted trial rate for the baseline and bill bursts separately. We'll show projected unit economics per 1k requests for each config.
[03:36] Omar: For fallback policy, who controls rollout? We need canary vs full deploy options and automatic fallback if p95 exceeds threshold.
[03:44] Diego: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B and automatic fallback policies — you set SLOs and it can route to fallback model variant automatically. We'll demo that.
[03:52] Lena: Do you support region routing? We have EU users and need data residency for them.
[03:56] Maya: Yes, routing by policy (latency, cost, region) is supported. For EU you can pin models to region or use private deployment in-region.
[04:05] Harriet: On network — VPC peering and egress rules: do you need a VPN or just peering?
[04:10] Diego: Peering is typically enough; for on-prem we support private deployment with deployed control plane. We'll itemize required firewall rules in the ops doc.
[04:20] Omar: Any known gotchas? For example, long token contexts causing KV cache thrash?
[04:24] Diego: We test for cache thrash in bench; also smart routing and prefix caching reduce repeated work. We'll include a regression test set.
[04:31] Lena: Bench specifics — we need p95 latency for short chat under 350ms at 120 RPS steady, and survival under 1.2k burst with degradation gracefully. Also cost per 1k requests target of $X (we'll fill number).
[04:42] Maya: We'll map to your token mix and provide numbers for baseline reserved pool (N A100s), burst pool (M smaller instances or warm small M60s) and a fallback policy.
[04:51] Omar: Can you run a dry-run with synthetic load first and then real traces?
[04:55] Diego: Yes, synthetic then sanitized traces. We'll do cold/warm paths.
[05:00] Harriet: For the POC environment, who will own infra changes? Our SREs will need to approve peering and KMS access.
[05:05] Maya: We'll coordinate with Harriet and provide a checklist.
[05:09] Lena: Are you able to emulate our nightly batch summary load to measure memory pressure?
[05:14] Diego: We'll craft a trace to hit long sequences and watch for OOMs; part of the bench is memory telemetry.
[05:20] Omar: Ok cool. Can you also include guidance on quantization levels and expected perf delta?
[05:24] Diego: Sure — we'll present FP16 vs 8-bit quant tradeoffs and show expected latency and quality deltas using your eval prompts.
[05:31] Maya: Quick note — we'll also include a rollback playbook: how we drop to smaller model, throttle batch jobs, and alert ops.
[05:37] Harriet: That helps. For timeline — once we get the sanitized trace, how quickly can you spin up a bench env?
[05:42] Diego: Assuming peering and credentials within 48 hours, we'll have bench env in 72 hours. The first bench run can be done in week 1.
[05:49] Lena: Ok, let's confirm initial capacity numbers — what's your recommendation for reserved GPUs to handle 120 RPS with our mix?
[05:56] Diego: Preliminary: 6x A100 (40GB) for steady-state for the primary model family, with 2x smaller units pre-warmed for bursts. But that's a starting point — bench will tune.
[06:08] Omar: Could you also provide an H100 estimate?
[06:10] Diego: Yes — H100 would likely reduce latency ~20–30% but cost is higher; we'll provide both.
[06:16] Lena: Ok, let's make sure the SOW calls out explicit success criteria, measurement methodology, and the decision gates.
[06:22] Maya: We'll draft SOW with those gates: pass/fail criteria and stop conditions.
[06:26] [unclear speaker]: (mumble) —
[06:30] Maya: Any other security requirements we should know?
[06:32] Harriet: Retention window for logs is strict — 30 days max. Also need field-level encryption for sensitive tokens.
[06:38] Diego: We'll note that.
[06:40] Omar: One more Q — are you able to show cost sensitivity for autoscale aggressiveness? Like keep more warm instances vs spin on demand.
[06:47] Maya: Yes we'll include a cost/latency curve for multiple autoscale configs.
[06:51] Lena: Great. I think that's it from our side.
[06:54] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send SOW + bench template, Diego to prepare bench script, Drawbridge to send sanitized trace and approve peering. We'll aim for bench env in 72 hours after creds.
[07:05] Omar: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[07:08] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the sizing workshop.

End of transcript.

Notes on audio/transcription quality: speaker labels occasionally overlap and small words misheard (e.g., "Redwood Dedicated" sometimes transcribed as "red wood dedicated").
